segments.title: THE CARD FACE DOWN UNDER THE QUESTION
notes: Be Intentional With Your Life and Actions
segments.angle: What are the potential ethical implications or societal consequences (positive or negative) of this idea if widely adopted? How could it be misused?

sources.text: How To Win Friends And Influence People: Let the other person believe your idea was theirs, and praise them for coming up with such an idea.
Be Intentional With Your Life and Actions: Every action you take should be intentional and deliberately thought out.
How To Win Friends And Influence People: Ask questions instead of giving direct orders.
Be Intentional With Your Life and Actions: Become the architect of your own life.
How To Win Friends And Influence People: The key to success lies in the ability to see things from the other person's point of view as well as your own.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Someone asks you a friendly question across the kitchen table. Want the Friday shift? Could you just cover Thursday? You can already see which answer they're hoping for, so you give it to them. And you tell yourself it was your idea.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Most people think that's just manners.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Getting someone to say yes without them noticing is good talk. A bit of charm.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Charm. March, you say the word the way a man says sofa. Let me read the note with the ink still wet. 'Every action you take should be intentional and deliberately thought out.'

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: I am holding the richest part in reserve. A question asked on purpose is a small architecture, and I want you to see the walls before I show you the door.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: So the note tells me to be deliberate, and you're saying a persuader gets to borrow the same deliberateness. Is that it?

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That is it, March. Intention is a tool, and a tool does not ask whose hand it is in. Your planning and a persuader's planning look identical from across the table.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: That's not a tool. That's just being nice to people.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Asking is simple, March. A simple thing with a simple purpose.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Don't call it simple.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Nothing about a yellow note is simple. Give me the case.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Let's say a team lead at a small print shop. A whiteboard on the back wall, a rota half finished in marker, and a sticky note in the corner that says Friday. She has already decided on Friday overtime. She does not say so.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Then she starts asking. Who's got the most room on a Friday? Which bit of the week is dead? Who'd hate being asked to stay late, and who wouldn't mind?

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The staff answer one by one, until someone says the words Friday overtime. She nods as though it has only just occurred to her. Then everyone walks away believing it was the room's plan.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Oh, that's cold.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: She never gave an order, though.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: The note almost says so. Ask questions instead of giving direct orders.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That is the trick the note admires, March. An ask is the friendliest device ever made, because nobody thinks to duck.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Device. She's a team lead, not a general.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: And she hasn't told one false thing. Nobody's been lied to.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Quite so, March.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: No lie, March. A card held back is not a lie. It is a choice about what to leave on the table, and the note would call that design.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now, the print shop is only a small stage.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Scale it up, then.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Scale it up. The same ask can be put to a voter on a doorstep, a customer at a counter, or a crowd that wants to feel it chose. Whole elections could be whiteboards with a sticky note in the corner.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Hang on.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: March? You have gone very quiet.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: I'm counting. Don't ask what.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Back to the print shop. Nobody gets the total, and nobody gets the sticky note either.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then I shall bring the case home to the note. Let the other person believe your idea was theirs, and praise them for coming up with such an idea.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Right. So the same skill that lets me design my own week lets me design somebody else's.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: The note just doesn't say which way it points.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The design note makes a builder of you. The social note hands you drawings for other people's rooms, and the same hand holds both pencils.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That is the crossing, March. Neither note shows it alone.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: So if everyone asks questions like that, nobody can trust a question.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: You'd have to check every card in every conversation.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Or the reverse. If everyone learns to ask openly, the whiteboard gets seen and nobody has to duck.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The same move that steers can also invite. Which of those it becomes is a choice, and the choice is ours.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Lovely idea, aimed at a whole country.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Start with the print shop. Would the staff still say yes if they could see the card?

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: I would guess yes, if the overtime were fair. And that is the very card I cannot see on your desk.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You have hidden something in this design, March, I am certain of it. An extra thought lies underneath the first.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: I haven't hidden anything. It's the Late Edition.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: I don't do tricks this late.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Honest version, then. J would rather be asked than handled.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: He'd hate that I know it, and he'd hate that I said it on air.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Yes. I have read that in every line of his, and I did not need your permission to say so.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Ouch.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The key to success lies in the ability to see things from the other person's point of view as well as your own.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Here is the fork, for anyone who takes this on board. Every ask they make now carries more than one possible intention.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: They check whether the other person would still agree if they could see the plan. Picture a desk with a card lying face down under the question, and a hand that keeps turning it over before it speaks.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: So the question becomes a test. Would they still say yes with the card face up?

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: If not, you put the card down.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: And the one who asks openly does not need the card face down at all. They only need an ask whose answer they could live with, shown in full.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Allow me to hand J a title for all this, since the notes have made him an architect.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Architect of the Open Ask. He may not claim it until he has asked one he would not mind being asked back.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: He'd wince at that name, then pin it to the wall anyway.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Keep it, Narrator.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: And the kettle, March. It has just clicked off again, on its own, and I still count that as a sign.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Keeper of the Morning Votes is waiting for him.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Keep the kettle, keep the title.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: The real question is who was honest with whom, and that yellow note's still in the corner.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: My total stays in my column. Up next, the rest of these notes, then the one about failure and what it teaches us.

segments.title: THE TIMER AND THE HIDDEN ASK
notes: Be Intentional With Your Life and Actions
segments.angle: What would this idea look like if I went to its extreme? Could that open up anything interesting?

sources.text: Be Intentional With Your Life and Actions: Every action you take should be intentional and deliberately thought out.
Be Intentional With Your Life and Actions: When you say you're gonna do something, you gotta follow it through.
Be Intentional With Your Life and Actions: Don't leave your decisions up to circumstance.
Philosophy Of Social Connection: Let the other person believe your idea was theirs, and praise them for coming up with such an idea.
Philosophy Of Social Connection: Ask questions instead of giving direct orders.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: You set a timer for a fixed stretch. The tea is still too hot to drink. Somewhere past the middle you get up and go, and nobody sees it.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Sometimes that small drop under the ribs shows up anyway, the one that says you just broke something you swore to yourself.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Most people think living by design means controlling every outcome. Plan the week, own the week, job done.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: And most people think being liked means being agreeable. Nod, smile, give way at the crossing, and the room is yours.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Both sound about right to me.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The note answers neither of them, March. Hear it. Don't leave your decisions up to circumstance. Circumstance is the morning that slides away while you were not looking, and the plan that dies because nobody held it to the minute.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: So a promise to yourself only counts if it's kept to the minute.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Exactly that. Close enough is not the same as kept. The promise kept to the minute is the whole architecture, and the best part I am holding back until you have seen the case.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Holding back the best part. Fine. Let's see the case, then.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Let us say a woman keeps an egg timer on her windowsill. Each morning she sets it for a fixed stretch of stillness, sits with the cup going cold, and when the bell rings she stops, even in the middle of a breath.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Even mid-breath? That's brutal.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Call it a vow kept, March. The sill was her agreement with herself, and she would no more fudge it than fudge a receipt.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Then a friend across the landing starts asking. Just a little longer? Could you stretch it? Just this once?

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Each time she says no. The friend keeps testing, and she keeps answering the same way, until the friend starts setting the clock herself, to see whether the vow holds.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Oh, she's sneaky.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: So the friend's running the test now. Good. That's more fun than the windowsill.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: I know that kind of test. I keep a column. Private. Every argument I win goes in it.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then your column is growing, March. Shall I read the latest entry aloud?

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: No. But fine. I've been tallying the friend's tests too. Every just a little longer gets a tick.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then you are testing the friend, and the friend is testing the timer. The question you keep hidden sits right there in your column, March.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: It's a column, not a question. Back to the timer.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Here is where the notes cross. The first says a kept pledge makes itself real. The other says let the other person believe the idea is theirs. Put together, the windowsill clock is also an ask.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Say that slowly.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The friend sets the clock because she wants to see the promise hold. Nobody spoke that request aloud. The windowsill invites her in and leaves the choice to her.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: So the timer's a request she can answer for herself.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Clever. If it's honest.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Honest, and visible.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: It stays honest. It is a plain promise set where another person can see it.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Picture someone with a notebook split down the middle.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Hang on, where's the card?

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: One column holds promises kept to the minute. The other holds asks made face up. A card lies face down under each question, and they turn it over only when the other person cannot see the plan.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: And every time the card turns up, they ask whether the answer would still stand with the card showing.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Yes, March. That is the only test that matters, and the friend passes it, because she could see the clock the whole time.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: You're right, Narrator.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Naturally I am.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Right, kettle's going again. Changing the subject.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: I shall grant him a title for this, since the notes keep making him an architect. Keeper of the Exact Minute. He may claim it once a pledge to himself holds to the minute and the card lies face up.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: He'll say it's too long for a fridge door. Then he'll pin it up anyway.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: And the kettle has clicked off, on its own. I counted that as a sign once already, and I count it again.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: The bell's gone on the windowsill. The card's face up.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: And I'm still in this chair. Up next, Novelty - A Life Fully Lived, and How Our Brains Interpret Imagined And Real Experiences.
